title: Projective domination of a proper morphism
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ be proper with $S$ qcqs. There are a proper surjection
$\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and a closed immersion
$i_S:\widetilde X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^n_S$ such that $f\pi=q_Si_S$, where
$q_S:\mathbf P^n_S\to S$ is the projection. Moreover

$$
i_X=(\pi,i_S):\widetilde X\hookrightarrow X\times_S\mathbf P^n_S=\mathbf P^n_X
$$

is a closed immersion. Both $\pi$ and $f\pi$ are projective.

The theorem holds over every qcqs base, in particular over every affine one,
with no Noetherian or finite-presentation assumption on $f$.

proof.text:
The version of Chow's lemma in Stacks 0202 gives a proper surjection
$\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and an immersion $i_S:\widetilde X\to\mathbf P^n_S$
for every separated finite-type $X\to S$ with $S$ qcqs. Here $f\pi$ is
proper. A map from a proper $S$-scheme to a separated $S$-scheme is proper:
its graph is closed and the projection of its product to the target is
proper. Therefore $i_S$ is proper. A proper immersion is a closed immersion.

For the second assertion factor $i_X$ as the graph of $\pi$ followed by the
base change of $i_S$:

$$
\widetilde X\longrightarrow\widetilde X\times_SX
\longrightarrow\mathbf P^n_S\times_SX .
$$

The first arrow is closed because $X\to S$ is separated, and the second is
closed because $i_S$ is. Their composite is $i_X$.

The form of Chow's lemma used here follows from the Noetherian one
([thm-chow-lemma]), even when $X\to S$ is not of finite presentation. Embed $X$
as a closed subscheme of a separated finitely presented $X_0$ by Stacks 01ZJ
([sk-prop-nagata-sketch-envelope]). Descend $X_0$ to a Noetherian stage
([sk-prop-nagata-sketch-approximation], [sk-prop-nagata-sketch-fp-models]),
apply the Noetherian form of Chow's lemma there, and base change its proper
surjective cover to $S$. Pull that cover back to the closed subscheme $X$.
The resulting source is closed in the source over $X_0$, so its map to
projective space is still an immersion, and properness and surjectivity of
its map to $X$ follow by base change.

Nagata's theorem and Chow's lemma play different roles. Nagata embeds $X$ as
an open subscheme of a proper scheme, keeping every point of $X$; it supplies
the compactifications and refinements used to define $Rf_!$. Chow replaces a
proper $X$ by a projective scheme mapping properly and surjectively onto it;
it supplies the projective morphisms $\pi$ and $f\pi$ in the reduction of
proper base change.

proof.text:
The version of Chow's lemma in Stacks 0202 gives a proper surjection
$\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and an immersion $i_S:\widetilde X\to\mathbf P^n_S$
over $S$ for every separated $X\to S$ of finite type with $S$ qcqs. Here
$f\pi$ is proper. A map from a proper $S$-scheme to a separated $S$-scheme is
proper, because its graph is closed and the projection of the product to the
target is proper. Therefore $i_S$ is a proper immersion, hence a closed
immersion.

For the second assertion, factor $i_X$ as the graph of $\pi$ followed by the
base change of $i_S$:

$$
\widetilde X\longrightarrow\widetilde X\times_SX\longrightarrow
\mathbf P^n_S\times_SX.
$$

The first arrow is closed because $X\to S$ is separated, and the second is
closed because $i_S$ is. Their composite is $i_X$. Hence $\pi$, which is $i_X$
followed by the projection $\mathbf P^n_X\to X$, and $f\pi=q_Si_S$ are
projective.

The form of Chow's lemma used here, for separated $X\to S$ of finite type over
a qcqs base, follows from the Noetherian one ([thm-chow-lemma]). Embed $X$ by
Stacks 01ZJ as a closed subscheme of some $X_0$ that is separated and of finite
presentation over $S$ ([prop-nagata-finite-type-closed-in-fp]), descend $X_0$ to a
Noetherian stage ([prop-nagata-noetherian-inverse-system], [lemma-nagata-separated-eventually]), apply the Noetherian
form of Chow's lemma there, and base change the resulting proper surjective
cover to $S$. Pulling this cover back to the closed subscheme $X$ gives a
source that is closed in the source of the cover of $X_0$, so its map to
projective space is still an immersion; its map to $X$ is proper and
surjective by base change.
